chunks: I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! When a woman waits for ten days and sees the blood, then she becomes clean and she waits for three days in a state of purity, then she sees the blood after that — should she withhold from the salat?' He said: 'No. This is a woman with istihadha (irregular bleeding). She should perform ghusl, insert cotton pad after cotton pad, combine the two prayers with one ghusl, and her husband may come to her if he so wishes.'

key_terms.تَجْمَعُ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ: Combining two prayers (typically Dhuhr-Asr or Maghrib-Isha) with a single ghusl, a concession for the woman with istihadha to ease the ritual burden
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: Classical Arabic formula of devotion meaning 'may I be made your sacrifice/ransom'; used as an expression of deep respect and submission when addressing the Imam
key_terms.مُسْتَحَاضَةٌ: A woman in a state of istihadha — irregular or inter-period vaginal bleeding that is not menstruation (haydh) or post-partum bleeding (nifas); carries different ritual obligations

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic rulings for a woman with istihadha who sees blood after ten days of menstruation and three days of purity?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a jurisprudential question posed to Imam Abu al-Hasan (AS) regarding a woman who experiences ten days of bleeding, followed by three days of purity, then bleeding again. The Imam rules this as istihadha (irregular bleeding, not haydh/menstruation), prescribing specific ritual obligations including ghusl, the use of cotton pads, combining two prayers with a single ghusl, and the permissibility of marital relations. This ruling reflects the Shia fiqh distinction between haydh (menstruation, which has a maximum of ten days) and istihadha (which continues after that limit), with different legal consequences for worship and marital obligations.
